frameworks.name: Failure Resume Building
frameworks.definition: A deliberate strategy of accumulating failures and learning from them to build credibility and capability; the more losses a person incurs, the greater their edge in future wins.

frameworks.name: Long-Tailed Distribution of Returns
frameworks.definition: In business, unlike baseball, a single success can generate exponentially greater returns than all prior failures combined; bold experimentation pays off when one outcome outweighs the cost of many experiments.

claims.text: Everyone loses before they win. No one wins on their first try; the first business is very unlikely to be the last, and the first product will be one the founder is embarrassed of years later.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Confidence is not a precondition for action; it is a retroactive result. After the first failure, the second attempt takes twice the emotional effort but half the actual effort, because the person now has realistic expectations and can quantify what is required to win.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Going from unknown optimism to known pessimism allows the person to grip the unknown and understand the true requirements for success, eliminating magical thinking.

numbers.axis: Effort ratio comparison between first and second attempts

claims.text: The best entrepreneurs in the world have the biggest failure resumes. Success requires building a failure resume, not avoiding losses.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Alex Hormozi has lost money on his first two real estate deals, almost lost all invested capital on crypto, lost money on bad hires (millions in hard costs), had six failed businesses, and nine failed partnerships.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: In business, unlike baseball, you only need to win once. A long-tailed distribution of returns means that when you swing, you can hit some home runs, but more importantly, one huge win can pay for many experiments.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: in entrepreneurial ventures with compounding returns
claims.mechanism: One massive success generates sufficient returns to cover all prior losses because the outcome distribution in business is unbounded, unlike baseball where maximum outcome is four runs.

claims.text: Big winners pay for many experiments in the form of failures and scars they incur and endure before hitting a win large enough that they never have to swing again.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: applies to entrepreneurs in high-upside ventures

claims.text: No matter where you are in your journey, you must believe with all your heart that you're going to make it, because no one else is going to believe for you. You cannot expect someone to invest in you more than you invest in yourself.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

claims.text: Some people say they would kill for a shot or die for a chance, when in reality they would not even wake up 60 minutes earlier for it. The disconnect between stated desire and actual behavior indicates a lack of genuine motivation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi

numbers.axis: Time investment as signal of true motivation

anchors.value: willing to die for a chance

examples.text: In The Matrix, Neo attempts to jump across buildings while everyone watches, believing he is the one. He falls on his first attempt. Cypher says 'everybody falls the first time,' emphasizing that even the person destined to become the one must fail first to achieve his goal.

Alex Hormozi found an old note from himself, 12 years old, setting a $10,000 per month income goal. Reading it years later, after achieving far greater success, brought him to tears because it represented the genuine commitment and belief he had at the start of his journey.

Hormozi lost money on his first two real estate deals and almost lost all invested capital. He also lost money on bad hires (millions in hard costs), had six failed businesses and nine failed partnerships. This experience exemplifies the failure resume required for entrepreneurial success.

practices.text: In 2025, if you start a podcast, start making content, start doing cold outbound, or take a new job, just start and accept that you will fail; focus on building your failure resume rather than avoiding mistakes.
Eliminate distractions and mental BS associated with not taking action; belief in yourself is the primary enabler of getting started.
